The lost surplus is a triangle with base <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>50</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>30</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50 - 30 = 20</annotation></semantics></math> and height from supply ($3) up to demand ($7) at 30 units: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="false"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mstyle><mo>×</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>40</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 4 = $40</annotation></semantics></math>.
A ceiling above the equilibrium price does not bind: the market already settles below it, so the price, quantity and surpluses are unchanged.
options: A ceiling holds the price down only when it sits below equilibrium.
A ceiling is a maximum, not a target.
At $2.00 the market already clears.
Right: a nonbinding ceiling has no effect.

why.correct: A binding limit on quantity (a quota) holds the quantity below equilibrium. With fewer fish sold, buyers bid the price up along demand: the price rises and the quantity falls to 600 tons, and the units no longer traded are deadweight loss.
options: Less fish for the same buyers pushes the price up.
A lower quantity moves buyers up along demand to a higher price.
Right: a binding quota cuts quantity and raises the price.
The licenses limit the total catch.

why.correct: Supply shifts right by the subsidy. Buyers pay a lower price than before and sellers receive a higher one (the price buyers pay plus the subsidy), so both sides share the benefit.
options: That is the effect of a tax.
Right: the subsidy opens a wedge with sellers on top.
Unless supply is perfectly elastic, sellers also gain part of it.
More quantity is sold only at a lower price to buyers.

why.correct: Above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded: a surplus of milk. Buyers pay more and buy less, so consumer surplus falls; the units no longer traded are deadweight loss.
options: Right: quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded.
Buyers buy less at the higher price.
The floor holds the price above equilibrium, so buyers pay more.
Buyers pay more and buy less, so consumer surplus falls.

why.correct: Tariff revenue is the tariff per unit times the imports after the tariff: the rectangle between the world price and the world price plus the tariff, over the gap between domestic quantity supplied and quantity demanded at the higher price. That is area e.
options: Those two triangles are the deadweight loss.
Those go to domestic producers as extra producer surplus.
Right: the tariff times the imports that remain.
That adds the deadweight loss triangles; only area e is collected.

why.correct: Area d is lost because domestic farms now make units that cost more than the world price; area f is lost because buyers no longer buy units they valued above the world price. Together, areas d and f.
options: Right: the two triangles.
Area e is tariff revenue, which the government collects.
Those are transfers to domestic producers.
Area a is consumer surplus that remains after the tariff.

why.correct: Domestic producers sell at the world price plus the tariff. Their surplus is the area above supply and below that price, out to the quantity they supply: areas b, c and g. At the world price alone it was area g.
options: That was producer surplus at the world price, before the tariff.
Area e goes to the government.
Area a is consumer surplus.
Right: above supply, below the higher price.

why.correct: At the world price, consumer surplus was areas a through f. With the tariff it is area a. Buyers lose areas b, c, d, e and f: part goes to producers (b and c), part to the government (e), and the rest is deadweight loss (d and f).
options: Area e is only the part that becomes tariff revenue.
Right: everything between the two prices under demand.
Those are only the parts no one gets.
That is only the part domestic producers gain.

why.correct: At $3, Dornians want 70 tons and Dornian farms supply 30. Imports fill the gap: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>70</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>30</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>40</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">70 - 30 = 40</annotation></semantics></math> tons.

At $4, Dornians want 60 tons and Dornian farms supply 40: imports fall to <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>60</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>40</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">60 - 40 = 20</annotation></semantics></math> tons.

Tariff revenue is the tariff times the imports after the tariff: <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mo>$</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>×</mo><mn>20</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">$1 \times 20 = $20</annotation></semantics></math>.

The gain from trade is the triangle between the domestic curves and the world price, from 30 tons to 70 tons: base 40 tons (the imports), height $5 minus $3. <math class="mic-m"><semantics><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="false"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mstyle><mo>×</mo><mn>40</mn><mo>×</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mo>$</mo><mn>40</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tfrac{1}{2} \times 40 \times $2 = $40</annotation></semantics></math>. (Consumer surplus rises from $125 to $245; producer surplus falls from $125 to $45.)
The world price ($240) is above Varrow's own price ($180). The price in Varrow rises to $240: farms supply more, buyers want less, and Varrow exports the difference.
options: Imports happen when the world price is below the domestic price.
Right: a world price above the domestic price means exports.
Farmers will not sell at home for $180 when they can get $240 abroad.
At $240 Varrow's farms supply more than its buyers want.

why.correct: The higher price raises producer surplus (farms sell more at $240) and lowers consumer surplus (buyers pay more and buy less). Producers gain more than consumers lose, so total surplus rises.
options: That happens when the world price is below the domestic price.
Buyers pay $60 more a ton.
Farmers sell more wheat at a higher price.
Right: the price rises to the world price.

why.correct: Total surplus rises. The gain to producers is larger than the loss to consumers by a triangle: the gain from trade on the wheat Varrow exports.
options: Right: the extra is the gain from trade.
The producers' gain includes the loss to consumers plus a triangle.
They do not cancel; the triangle of gains from trade is new.
Producers' gain equals consumers' loss plus the gain from trade.

why.correct: A country imports when the world price is below the price it would have without trade, so the world price line sits below the domestic equilibrium price.
Buyers pay the world price and buy the quantity demanded at it. Consumer surplus is the area under demand and above the world price, out to that larger quantity.
Producers sell at the world price and supply the quantity on supply at that price. Producer surplus is the area above supply and below the world price, out to that quantity.

Tariff revenue is the rectangle between the world price and the world price plus the tariff, over the imports that remain: from the quantity domestic firms supply to the quantity buyers demand at the higher price.

Two triangles: one between supply and the world price where domestic firms now produce units that cost more than imports, and one between demand and the world price where buyers give up units they valued above the world price.

With imports limited to 20 tons, the price in Dornia rises until domestic quantity demanded minus quantity supplied equals 20: at $4. Imports fall, domestic farms supply more, and buyers buy less. Unlike a tariff, the government collects no revenue from the quota itself.
options: With fewer imports at $3 there would be a shortage, so the price rises.
Fewer imports leave buyers competing for less rice.
Right: limiting imports raises the domestic price.
Imports were 40 tons; the quota cuts them.

why.correct: Other countries can supply the good at a lower opportunity cost: they have a comparative advantage in it. Buying at the lower world price lets the country use its own resources where it has a comparative advantage.
options: Domestic farms keep producing up to where supply meets the world price.
The world price comes from the world market.
Imports at a lower world price lower the domestic price.
Right: comparative advantage drives trade.

why.correct: The tariff raises the domestic price. Domestic producers sell more at a higher price, so they gain. Buyers pay more and buy less, and foreign sellers sell less into the country. (The government also collects revenue.)
options: They pay more and buy less.
Right: a higher price and more sales.
They sell fewer units into the country.

why.correct: Both raise the domestic price, raise domestic output, lower imports and create a deadweight loss. The difference is who gets the rectangle between the world price and the higher domestic price: with a tariff, the government collects it as revenue; with a quota, it goes to whoever holds the right to import.
options: Both raise the domestic price.
Both cut trade below free trade, so both create deadweight loss.
Right: the revenue rectangle is the difference.
Both lower imports.
